headline: Maine awards record $2.72M for winter warming shelters and 474 beds
dek: The MaineHousing grants will support 12 organizations in eight homeless-service hubs, but Bangor reporting shows that some local warming centers still face funding and capacity gaps.
body: MaineHousing has awarded $2,722,538 to 12 organizations that will provide 474 beds at short-term warming shelters this winter, the largest funding total and bed count since the state program began five years ago. The [Maine State Housing Authority's announcement](https://www.mainehousing.org/news/news-detail/2026/09/30/mainehousing-awards--2.72-million-for-winter-warming-shelters) says the grants reach eight of Maine's nine homeless-service hubs. Most of the shelters are expected to operate overnight through April 30, giving people experiencing homelessness or housing instability a place to get out of dangerous cold.

The awards are operating support, not a promise that 474 beds will be open every night regardless of weather or local staffing. MaineHousing says recipients may use the money for staff, supplies, transportation, longer hours and other shelter costs. Grant recipients will coordinate with municipalities, emergency managers and community partners when conditions become hazardous. That arrangement matters because a warming shelter is an emergency-weather resource, not the same thing as a permanent shelter or a year-round housing placement.

Bangor illustrates both the reach and the limits of the new round. The [Bangor Daily News reported](https://www.bangordailynews.com/2026/09/29/bangor/bangor-government/bangor-warming-centers-state-funding/) that The Brick Church will receive $427,650 to support 65 beds, while the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter will receive $10,000 for five beds. Together, the two awards total $437,650, more than any other Maine city received. The Mansion Church and Together Place also applied but were not awarded state funds, leaving uncertainty about how the city's full network will operate.

That uncertainty is tied to demand rather than just a budget line. Bangor's homeless response coordinator told the Bangor Daily News that the city's four warming centers served roughly 80 to 90 people per night last year. The report said the city had to provide emergency money last year after The Brick Church's request was denied, helping keep that center open and allowing Together Place to operate an overnight center for the first time. This year's larger state award improves the outlook for some sites, but it does not automatically cover every location that people may rely on during a cold snap.

Local operators told [WABI](https://www.wagmtv.com/2026/10/01/bangor-warming-shelters-prepare-winter-state-awards-record-grants/) that capacity remains a practical concern. Pastor Leon Licata of The Brick Church said the church can hold about 70 people, while 120 to 130 people were outside during one period last year. Pastor Terry Dinkins of The Mansion Church said his center plans to open even without a state grant, though it may need community donations and other changes to keep doing so. Those accounts describe local plans and reported conditions; they are not a statewide count of unmet shelter demand.

MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said dangerous winter weather can put people at risk, particularly those without stable housing. The agency's broader winter guidance also points to the Home Energy Assistance Program and Energy Crisis Intervention Program for eligible households that need help with heating costs or an emergency. Those programs address a different problem from a warming shelter: HEAP helps eligible homeowners and renters pay heating bills, while a warming center provides short-term space when cold, wind or precipitation creates an immediate safety risk.

The [Maine Department of Energy Resources' winter-resources page](https://www1.maine.gov/energy/winter-heating-resources) says warming centers are normally opened for a specific emergency or event when temperatures, wind chill or precipitation may become dangerous. The department directs residents to the Maine Emergency Management Agency's statewide list when centers are operating. It also says HEAP applications are distributed through nine Community Action Agencies and that households should seek assistance before a heating emergency. Availability, eligibility and opening times can vary by community, so the statewide grant total should not be read as a single hotline or guaranteed bed for every resident.

The immediate takeaway is that Maine is putting more money into winter shelter operations before the cold season, while the Bangor experience shows why the network still needs local coordination and backup funding. The 12 awardees will determine how their grants translate into staffing, transportation, supplies and hours, and communities will work with emergency officials as conditions change. For people who may need help, the next step is to check local warming-center information early and contact a Community Action Agency about heating assistance rather than wait for fuel or weather conditions to become an emergency.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Maine awards record $2.72M for winter warming shelters
seoDescription: MaineHousing awarded $2.72 million for 474 warming-shelter beds, while Bangor providers still face gaps in funding and capacity.
